extracted.intended_audience: computer science students and programmers learning literate programming, software documentation, user-manual design, and academic refereeing
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture-note style guidelines for writing literate programs (WEB), naming modules/identifiers, structuring modules and error handling, preparing user manuals, and good refereeing practices for academic papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural order of exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Present program constructs in the same order in which the creator made decisions about them; there is a natural order of exposition that matches reading and writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don felt it was clear what had to be presented next throughout composition; use this natural ordering to present program constructs so readers follow the author's decision process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of personification
rubrics_metrics.description: Be consistent about whether the program is described as autonomous or acted upon (e.g., use 'we insert the element' vs 'it inserts the element').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don favours 'we' for exposition; consistency matters. There is also a position favoring the computer saying 'I' when referring to itself—acceptable but contested (Dijkstra dislikes it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Module naming: imperatives vs descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Name action modules with imperatives (e.g., 'Store the word in the dictionary') and declarative/listing modules with descriptors (e.g., 'Procedures for sorting').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imperatives work better for modules that perform actions; descriptors are appropriate for modules that are declarative in function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize module names (first letter)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is natural to capitalize the first letter of a module name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capitalization consistently for module names to improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifier styling and compound words
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid awkward internal capitalization like 'FindinNew Word3'; use a short underscore to conjoin words (e.g., 'get_word').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WEB allows underscores to conjoin words (TANGLE may remove it for compilers); be aware Pascal may not accept some identifier forms. Long descriptive identifiers (40 characters) are acceptable if meaning is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module description: high-level intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Each module should contain an informal but clear description of what it actually does, conveying high-level intuition rather than a play-by-play account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid a simple step-through of the algorithm; a high-level account is much more helpful to convey what is going on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module length and decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Modules should be short—about a dozen lines is suggested; if a module is too long, cut it into several manageable pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The WEB philosophy is to break complex things into tractable parts; once adopted, programming in small modules becomes easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'engineerese' and poor punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't slip into terse conjunction-only prose without punctuation ('engineerese'); this makes poor documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good punctuation and readable prose are necessary for effective documentation; Joyce-like stream-of-consciousness is not appropriate for docs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drop obsolete conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: When adopting a new style (e.g., WEB), do not carry along inappropriate older conventions (e.g., putting comments after each 'end' to show what was ended).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify conventions that are unnecessary in the new style and avoid them to prevent clutter and confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person/voice choices (I vs we vs it)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose how you personify the computer (we, it, I) and be consistent; opinions differ on which is best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don generally likes 'we' and sometimes 'I' for the computer; avoid mixing 'it' and 'we' inconsistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't start sentences with symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid beginning a sentence with a symbol (e.g., 'data assumes that ...'); rewrite to start with words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As in mathematics, starting sentences with symbols should be avoided because they are awkward to read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive variable names and precision of terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use descriptive names (e.g., 'caps_range' instead of 'range') and be precise with vocabulary ('complement' vs 'component').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good naming helps exposition and reader understanding; avoid ambiguous or terse names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nouns for data, verbs for procedures (Truth in Naming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let function determine part of speech: use nouns for data and verbs/imperatives for procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a placeholder variable should be a noun (e.g., 'place') rather than a verb; verbs are for procedures, not data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment on variable declarations placed mid-program
rubrics_metrics.description: When declaring variables at any point in the program (allowed in WEB), add a comment even if only cursory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps readers who encounter declarations distributed through exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting conventions for symbols (asterisks, hex)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful with typeset asterisks (they print higher than typewritten ones); prefer 'x' for multiplication and use typewriter font for hex numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a typewriter-style font with body-centered dots for multiplication and typewriter font for hexadecimal identifiers (e.g., typeset '3F' in typewriter, leave '63' normal) for subliminal type-checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group specialized routines together
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep routines that use a specialized data structure (e.g., heap routines) together in the text so they can be read as a group while fresh in the reader's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WEB allows flexible ordering; exploit it to colocate related routines rather than scattering them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module title capitalization style
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid capitalizing every word in module titles; better to capitalize only the first word (newspaper-headline vs sentence style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalizing odd small words (and, the) looks unnatural—prefer only initial capitalization for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocabulary consistency between docs and program
rubrics_metrics.description: Words used in the documentation should match the words used in the formal program; using two different terms for the same thing confuses readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure terminology alignment between prose and code identifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of begins/ends: put them in called modules
rubrics_metrics.description: Put begins and ends inside the called modules rather than in the calling module to avoid mixing conventions and bugs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example shows doing 'if down = 4 then (Punt); (Punt) = begin ... end' rather than placing begin/end around the call in the caller; mixing conventions can cause bugs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modularize error handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate error handling into its own modules referenced from the main flow to keep the main module focused on normal cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of embedding long error-handling code in a routine, use a short reference (e.g., '(Check if the data is wrong 28)') to point to a dedicated error module so the programmer stays motivated to do both normal and error code well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use italics for variable names in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use italics for variable names when they appear in comments to distinguish them from prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This typographic convention clarifies comments and matches variable mentions to declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module title variables should match local parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the variables in the module title correspond to the local parameters in the module itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This correspondence improves clarity and reduces cognitive load when reading module headings and bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technical phrases correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Only use technical phrases (e.g., 'tail recursion') when they correctly apply to the algorithm; mislabeling is misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases can impress but must be used in the proper context to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribute local variables for large procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: For large procedures, distribute local variable declarations as the exposition proceeds rather than gathering them all in one place far from use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fits WEB philosophy and improves local readability; variables should be close to their use.

rubrics_metrics.name: User manuals: avoid jargon and technical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't assume familiar CS terms ('Menu', 'Scrolling', 'Option-V') are transparent to naive users—use plain language or explain them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test manuals with truly naive users; terms familiar to CS people can be opaque to general users (Don's wife example).

rubrics_metrics.name: User manuals must explain how to escape/exit
rubrics_metrics.description: Always tell users how to get out of a mess or exit the program; this is commonly omitted but essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even a one-line exit description may be jargon; phrase it in plain language so novices can stop the program when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: User manual structure: overview, step-by-step, and skim-ability
rubrics_metrics.description: A good manual has a motivating introductory paragraph, a clear overview, step-by-step descriptions, crisp short sentences, helpful redundancy, and diagrams; it should be easy to skim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an overview and step-by-step instructions, diagrams, keyboard diagrams, and redundancy to aid different reading styles; anticipate readers starting in the middle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide interactive demonstrations and sensible defaults
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer an online demonstration ('type ?') to spare long descriptions and make terse manuals usable; default new inputs to the style of the preceding line rather than fixed defaults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interactive demos can replace verbose prose; reusing previous-line styles reduces user repetition and surprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear symbols/diagrams for controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a clear symbol to indicate modifier keys (e.g., control), diagrams of the keyboard, and emphasize holding the control key while typing another key.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state that modifier keys must be held, and use icons to describe scrolling directions (up/down/left/right) and other controls to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague/ambiguous phrasing in manuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace unclear advice like 'THIS IS VISIBLE HERE BUT NOT HERE' with explicit instructions (e.g., 'Extra long messages can be seen if you make them move').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be concrete and actionable rather than cryptic; explain behavior rather than pointing out visibility differences without instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendly tone and honest reassurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Include encouraging comments like 'Good luck!' and 'Enjoy', but avoid meaningless or misleading reassurance (e.g., 'this system has been carefully redesigned not to bite').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendly tone helps, but avoid platitudes that may reduce trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check galley proofs carefully and respond to copy-edit changes
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewing galley proofs, verify substitutions and corrections (copy-editor changes), respond to queries (e.g., 'OK?'), and be prepared to approve or correct inserted changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of copy-editor substitutions (e.g., 'cleverer' vs 'more clever'); check camera copy vs laser output notes; act within publisher deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include sufficient bibliographic details
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide bibliographic details editors request (e.g., conference location and date) because libraries/indexers may index conferences by city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although some style guides suggest omission, including location helps indexing and prevents propagation of bibliographic errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing: prioritize originality
rubrics_metrics.description: The first criterion for referees is originality: determine whether the material is a genuine advance on previous work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees should judge whether the paper makes a real contribution beyond prior literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referees' duty to authors and readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees' primary responsibility is to authors and readers, not just to editors or career advancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees should aim to advance science and good exposition, helping authors produce work that readers can build upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referees should be teachers and constructive
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should supply constructive criticism and try to help authors improve their writing, avoiding tasteless anonymous attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive comments can transform an author's career; anonymity should not be used to be needlessly harsh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referees should improve technical quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees can and should contribute to the technical improvement of a paper by providing references, pointing out related work, and suggesting or supplying improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees have been known to contribute results or theorems anonymously; supplying useful references and identifying subtle technical errors is valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose journals for quality of referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should choose journals with the best referees (not simply the least critical editor) to ensure meaningful review and validation of contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A journal with knowledgeable referees helps authors know whether they truly made a contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on content before grammar when content is poor
rubrics_metrics.description: If a paper's content is obviously bad, do not spend time on grammar; conversely, if the content has merit, help ensure it is well expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate reviewing effort proportionally: substantive contributions deserve attention to exposition too.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear referee recommendation categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Referee reports may use explicit overall ratings (accept, accept with minor changes, accept with major modifications, reject) and may suggest alternate journals for rejected work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This downward filtering helps place papers at an appropriate venue; some review forms include checkboxes to standardize recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warn against 'facile generalizations'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid proposing mechanical 'generalizations' that are merely routine manipulations and do not create new insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek generalizations that add conceptual value rather than trivial extensions of arguments.
